code.title: Class vs object: references and identity
code.python:
class Dog:
    # The class is the blueprint; each Dog(...) call makes one object.
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

d1 = Dog("Rex", 3)
d2 = d1               # second reference to the SAME object
d3 = Dog("Rex", 3)    # a different object with equal data
d2.age += 1           # visible through d1 as well
print("d1", d1.name, d1.age)
print("d3", d3.name, d3.age)
# "is" compares identity, not content
print("d1 and d2 same object:", str(d1 is d2).lower())
print("d1 and d3 same object:", str(d1 is d3).lower())

followUps:
Identity asks "is it the very same object?", equality asks "do two objects hold the same data?". Identity is the reference or address; equality is a rule you define.

Java: == is identity, equals is content (if you override it). Python: is is identity, == calls __eq__. JavaScript: === on objects is identity only. C++: == on objects calls your operator==; identity is comparing addresses (&a == &b). Example: two Dog("Rex", 3) objects are equal but not identical. If you override equality, override hashCode (or __hash__) too.

Objects live in memory the program manages, and they go away when nothing can reach them (garbage collection) or when you destroy them yourself (C++).

Java, Python, JavaScript and C#: objects live on a heap; local variables hold references on the stack. A garbage collector frees an object once no reference reaches it, at a time you do not control (Python also frees at once when its reference count hits 0). C++: an object can be on the stack (destroyed at the closing brace) or on the heap via new or smart pointers; unique_ptr destroys it when the owner goes out of scope. Forgetting to release a heap object in C++ is a leak.

code.title: Composition vs aggregation: who owns the part

followUps:
A composed part usually becomes a table with a foreign key to the whole, set to cascade delete, so deleting the whole deletes its parts.

Example: order_line(id, order_id NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, sku, qty). The NOT NULL says a line cannot exist without an order, and the cascade matches "part dies with the whole". For aggregation the foreign key is nullable (a player may have no team) and uses ON DELETE SET NULL or no cascade, because the part outlives the whole. Small value-like parts can also be embedded as columns or a JSON column of the owner row.

Sometimes yes, but only when the difference changes code; otherwise plain association is enough and the debate wastes time.

The distinction matters in two places: lifecycle (who deletes the parts? cascade or not) and ownership (may the part be shared or leak out?). If a Team is deleted, you must decide what happens to its Players; that is the aggregation question. UML itself says aggregation has almost no precise semantics, and many teams draw only association and composition. In an interview, say "I show composition when the part dies with the whole and use a plain line otherwise", and move on.

code.title: Encapsulation, abstraction and polymorphism together

followUps:
Inheritance hurts when a subclass inherits behaviour it cannot honour, or when it is used only to reuse code and the two classes are not really the same kind.

Classic case: Stack extends ArrayList (Java's old Stack extends Vector is a real one). A stack should only push and pop, but now callers can insert in the middle and break the stack rule. Another: Penguin extends Bird with fly() throwing. Fix by composition: Stack holds a list privately and exposes only push and pop.

No. A getter and setter for every field is almost the same as public fields, because outsiders can still set any value and the class cannot protect its rules.

Real encapsulation exposes behaviour, not raw state. Instead of getBalance() followed by setBalance(b - 50), offer withdraw(50) that checks the limit and keeps the invariant. Read-only getters for values callers genuinely need are fine, but returning a mutable internal list is a leak. Ask for each field: does anyone outside need it? If not, keep it private with no getter.

Give each class one clear job, put each action on the class that owns the data, and keep the "system" class to coordination only.

Test: if a method mostly reads another class's fields, move it there. Example: instead of LibrarySystem.calcFine(loan), write loan.fine(today), since Loan owns the due date. Then LibrarySystem is left with just checkout(member, book), which calls the objects that own the rules. A rough smell: a class with more than about 7 methods that name different nouns, or one that every other class depends on.

An actor becomes a class only when the system stores data about it or it has behaviour the system must model; otherwise it is just a caller outside the system.

Example: in a parking lot, a Driver who only arrives and leaves is not needed; the Vehicle and Ticket are. But a Member of a library has a loan limit, a name and borrowed books, so Member is a class. In a ride-hailing app, Driver has a rating, location and status, so it is a class. Ask: does the system keep state or enforce rules for this actor? If yes, class; if it only triggers use cases, leave it out.

code.title: Interface contract plus abstract base class

followUps:
The compiler refuses to compile the class until it picks a side, because it cannot guess which default method you want.

In Java, if A and B both have default void hi() and C implements A, B, then C must override hi(). It can choose one explicitly: public void hi() { A.super.hi(); }. This avoids the old diamond problem by forcing a decision. If one interface extends the other, the more specific one wins and no error occurs.

Choose a sealed interface when the full list of variants is known and closed, so the compiler can check you handled every one.

Example: sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square with records for each. A switch over a Shape without a default then fails to compile if you add a Triangle and forget a case. Use a normal interface instead when third parties must add new implementations (a plugin point such as PaymentMethod). Sealed gives safe exhaustive logic; open interfaces give extensibility.

code.title: Composition over inheritance: swap a pay policy

followUps:
It is the problem that a harmless-looking change in a parent class silently breaks its subclasses, because they depend on how the parent works inside.

Example: a CountingList extends ArrayList overrides add and addAll to count items. But ArrayList.addAll may call add for each item, so adding 3 items counts 6. The subclass broke on an internal detail. Composition avoids it: CountingList holds a list and forwards calls, so only the public contract matters.

Strategy is composition over inheritance applied to one behaviour: the object holds a small interchangeable object and delegates to it instead of subclassing to vary behaviour.

In the payroll example, PayPolicy is the strategy interface, Salaried and Hourly are concrete strategies, and Employee is the context. Changing a policy at runtime is one assignment: e.changePolicy(new Hourly(20)). With inheritance you would need a new class for each combination and a new object to switch.

The most common mistakes are wrong arrow types, missing multiplicities, and drawing every detail so the picture is unreadable.

Typical errors: using an arrowhead for inheritance in the wrong direction (the hollow triangle points at the parent); mixing up filled diamond (composition) and hollow diamond (aggregation); putting the diamond on the part's end instead of the whole's end; leaving out 1, 0..* and 1..*; showing both a field and an association line for the same link; and listing getters, setters and constructors. Keep it to classes, key fields, key methods and correct lines.

A domain model shows the business concepts and their rules in the customer's words; a design model shows the classes you will actually code, including technical ones.

Domain model for a library: Member, Book, Loan, Fine. The design model adds things like LoanRepository, FinePolicy interface, and an EmailNotifier, plus types and method signatures. Start with the domain model to agree on meaning, then refine it into the design model. In a short interview they usually merge into one diagram, but say which parts are business concepts and which are your technical additions.

Draw the call to the email service as an asynchronous message (open arrowhead) and show the caller continuing without waiting for a reply.

Example: OrderService places the order, sends an open-arrow sendEmail(order) to a Mailer lifeline (or a queue), and immediately returns confirmation to the user. The email processing happens later on its own activation bar. If a failure matters, add a separate message from the mailer back, such as deliveryFailed, or a retry loop on the queue side. The point is that no dashed return arrow blocks the caller.

Draw a compensation: when payment fails, the system must undo the earlier reservation by calling release on inventory.

Steps: OrderService calls inventory.reserve(sku, 2) and it succeeds; payment.charge(card, 50) returns failure; an alt fragment with the guard [payment failed] then sends inventory.release(sku, 2) and returns "order failed" to the user. Without the release call, stock would stay locked. This also reveals the need for the release method on Inventory and for idempotent retries.

code.title: Keep a two-way association consistent
code.python:
class Course:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self._students = []
    # Underscore-prefixed: only Student calls these, so both sides stay in sync.
    def _add_internal(self, s): self._students.append(s)
    def _remove_internal(self, s): self._students.remove(s)
    def roster(self): return "[" + ", ".join(s.name for s in self._students) + "]"

class Student:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self._courses = []
    # Single entry point: updates both sides together.
    def enroll(self, c):
        self._courses.append(c)
        c._add_internal(self)
    def drop(self, c):
        self._courses.remove(c)
        c._remove_internal(self)
    def list(self): return "[" + ", ".join(c.name for c in self._courses) + "]"

ann, bob = Student("Ann"), Student("Bob")
math, art = Course("Math"), Course("Art")
ann.enroll(math); ann.enroll(art); bob.enroll(math)
print("Ann courses: " + ann.list())
print("Math students: " + math.roster())
ann.drop(math)
print("After Ann drops Math: " + math.roster())

followUps:
In JPA the "owning side" is the side whose table holds the foreign key, and mappedBy marks the other side as a read-only mirror; you must still keep both Java objects in sync yourself.

Example: Order has @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order") List<Line> lines, and Line has @ManyToOne Order order. Only line.order is written to the database. If you add a line to order.lines without setting line.order, nothing is saved. So write a helper order.addLine(line) that sets both, which is exactly the single entry point idea.

If two objects reference each other and equals or hashCode use those references, the calls recurse forever and end with a stack overflow.

Example: Student.hashCode() hashes its courses, and each Course.hashCode() hashes its students, so computing one hash calls the other, then back again, without end. The same happens with toString and JSON serialisation. Fix: base equals and hashCode only on the id (or a few stable fields) and leave out the back-reference, and exclude one side from toString and JSON.

code.title: Liskov violation (Square) and the fix
code.python:
class Rectangle:
    def __init__(self): self.w = 0; self.h = 0
    def set_width(self, w): self.w = w
    def set_height(self, h): self.h = h
    def area(self): return self.w * self.h

# Violation: a Square keeps both sides equal, so callers get surprised.
class Square(Rectangle):
    def set_width(self, x): self.w = x; self.h = x
    def set_height(self, x): self.w = x; self.h = x

# This code is correct for any Rectangle: width 5, height 4 means area 20.
def resize_and_measure(r):
    r.set_width(5)
    r.set_height(4)
    return r.area()

# Fix: separate immutable shapes with one shared method.
class Rect:
    def __init__(self, w, h): self.w = w; self.h = h
    def area(self): return self.w * self.h

class Sq:
    def __init__(self, side): self.side = side
    def area(self): return self.side * self.side

print("Violation: Rectangle -> " + str(resize_and_measure(Rectangle())))
print("Violation: Square -> " + str(resize_and_measure(Square())) + " (expected 20)")
print("Fix: Rect 5x4 -> " + str(Rect(5, 4).area()) + ", Square 4 -> " + str(Sq(4).area()))

followUps:
An overriding method may not throw broader checked exceptions than the parent, and its return type may be narrower (covariant); both are LSP rules in the language.

Parent Shape get() can be overridden as Circle get() because every caller expecting a Shape still works. Parent void read() throws IOException may be overridden to throw FileNotFoundException or nothing, but not Exception, since callers only handle IOException. The compiler enforces the checked-exception rule but not unchecked ones, so a subclass that adds new unchecked failures still breaks LSP silently.

Yes, because with no setters the problem of changing one side disappears: nothing can be set, so the parent's promise cannot be broken.

An immutable Rectangle(w, h) with a Square(side) that passes side, side to the parent keeps area = w * h true for every object. Trouble returns if the parent has methods like withWidth(w) that return a new rectangle: for a square that would have to return a non-square. So it is safe only while the contract has no width-only changes. Many designers still prefer separate classes behind a Shape interface for simplicity.

code.title: Value object vs double, entity by id

followUps:
A double stores binary fractions, so many decimal amounts cannot be stored exactly and small errors build up.

In the program, 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, so comparing it with 0.3 is false. Across thousands of transactions, such errors cause totals that are off by a cent. Use integer cents (long) or a decimal type (BigDecimal, decimal, Python Decimal) with an explicit rounding rule, and wrap it in a Money class that also carries the currency.

Primitive obsession means passing raw ints and strings for concepts that have rules; a value object gives each concept its own type so mistakes are caught and the rules live in one place.

Example: transfer(int from, int to, int amount) lets you swap arguments by mistake without any compiler error. With transfer(AccountId from, AccountId to, Money amount) the swap will not compile, and Money can refuse negative values and mismatched currencies in its constructor. Email, PhoneNumber and DateRange follow the same idea: validate once, use everywhere.

code.title: Extensible design: new pricing policy, hotel chain

followUps:
I create a variation point only for things the requirements said might change, or where the cost of adding it later is high; everything else stays simple.

Rules of thumb: ask the interviewer "which parts will vary?"; wrap rules that are policies (pricing, discounts, matching) behind an interface; keep stable data as plain fields. Example: "hotel rates differ by season" is stated, so PricingPolicy; "hotel name" is not a policy. Three real variants justify an abstraction; one guess does not (YAGNI).

Say the assumption broke, name what changes, and show the smallest redesign instead of pretending the old model still fits.

Example: bookings were by night, and now by hour. The Booking held two dates; I would replace them with a TimeRange value object (start and end instant), and make PricingPolicy.price(range) take it. Nights become one special case of range. Rooms, hotels and policies stay. I would also point out which tests change (overlap and price tests) so the interviewer sees control over the impact.

code.title: Leaky getter vs defensive copy
code.python:
class Book:
    def __init__(self):
        self._copies = ["copy-1"]
    # Leaky: hands out the internal list, so callers can change it.
    def leaky_copies(self): return self._copies
    # Safe: hands out a copy; the internal list stays under the class's control.
    def safe_copies(self): return list(self._copies)
    def size(self): return len(self._copies)

a = Book()
a.leaky_copies().append("hacked")     # outside code edits the internals
print("leaky: internal size after outside add = " + str(a.size()))
b = Book()
b.safe_copies().append("hacked")      # only changes the throwaway copy
print("safe: internal size after outside add = " + str(b.size()))

followUps:
Give it the actors, the rules and the constraints, and ask for a design in a stated shape so you can check it quickly.

Useful parts: the requirements paragraph, the 3 to 5 key rules (loan limit 3, fine 2 per day), the scope (no reservations), the language and the style (small classes, composition, enums for statuses, money as integer cents, immutable value objects, no mutable collection getters). Ask for a class list with responsibilities first, then code, and say "list assumptions you made". Reviewing a short class list is faster than reviewing finished code.

Write the rules down as automatic checks that run in the build, and keep a short diagram next to the code that you update with each change.

ArchUnit (Java) tests can say "classes in domain must not depend on web" or "no class has more than 15 public methods", and the build fails if someone breaks it. Diagrams-as-code (PlantUML or Mermaid text in the repo) can be reviewed in pull requests, so a drifting design shows up as a diff. Add code review notes for ownership rules like "only Loan changes its due date".
